modalities.name: Plain Sensation Words
modalities.tagline: Your felt sense in plain body words, right now, on your own.
modalities.whatItIs: Plain Sensation Words is a new, untested concept that takes Focusing further away from guided imagery work. You attend to the vague bodily sense of your situation right now, but describe it only in plain sensation words such as tight, warm or heavy, with no pictures, stories or memories.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying with what the body is doing in the present, without turning it into images or history, may let a situation be felt freshly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for 10 to 15 minutes and ask how a current situation feels in your body right now. Each time a word comes, check that it names a sensation (pressure, flutter, ache) rather than a picture or a memory, and let the sensation be as it is without asking it to change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a simple self-led practice and find imagery or digging into the past tiring.
modalities.cautions: Even plain body attention can bring up strong feelings, so open your eyes or stop if it becomes too much. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified therapist, and this untested idea is not a substitute for treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Plain Sensation Words. You check how a situation feels in your body right now and describe it only in plain words like tight or warm. No images, no backstory. A simple, solo way to get clearer on what you feel.

modalities.name: How This Place Feels
modalities.tagline: Sense how the place you are in sits in your body.
modalities.whatItIs: How This Place Feels is a new concept that moves Focusing away from therapies built around inner parts and imagined figures, toward the real place you are in. Alone, you let a felt sense form of being in this particular room, street or building right now, and listen to what it says about your life there.
modalities.coreIdea: The places we spend time in carry a bodily feel of their own, and sensing it directly may show what a workplace, home or habit is really like for you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Wherever you are, a kitchen, an office or a bus, sit for 10 minutes with your eyes open, take in the space and ask "what is it like for me to be here?" Wait for a bodily answer (cramped, warm, buzzing, flat), find a word that fits and let it be, without deciding anything.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a quick, self-led way to notice how their surroundings affect them, for example before deciding whether to change jobs, rooms or routines.
modalities.cautions: Some places hold hard associations, so you can stop the exercise or leave the place if it stirs too much. It is an untested idea, and if a home or workplace feels unsafe, practical help and support matter more than any inner practice.
modalities.tweet: New concept: How This Place Feels. Wherever you are, kitchen, office or bus, pause and ask what it's like for your body to be here, then find one word that fits. A quick, solo way to notice how your surroundings sit with you.

modalities.name: Let the Body Choose
modalities.tagline: No topic, no steps, no goal: the body sets the agenda.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Body Choose is a new concept that strips Focusing of its steps and goals, moving it as far as possible from structured, agenda-led therapy. You pick no topic in advance; you lie down, wait, and whatever the body brings forward becomes the session.
modalities.coreIdea: Trusting the body to choose what needs attention, with no agenda and no aim to change it, may surface concerns a planned session would skip.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down somewhere quiet for 20 to 30 minutes with no topic and no technique. Wait until some bodily sense stands out and keep it company without trying to name or change it; if words or images arrive, welcome them, but they are not required.
modalities.whoItsFor: People worn out by worksheets, goals and self-improvement plans who want an open, body-led way to listen to themselves.
modalities.cautions: Without structure, unexpected feelings or memories can surface, so keep the freedom to sit up, open your eyes and stop. Anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should use it only with a qualified therapist, and it is an untested idea rather than a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Lie down with no topic, no steps and no goal, and keep company with whatever bodily sense stands out. That's Let the Body Choose, a new idea for people tired of worksheets and self-improvement plans.

modalities.name: How Old Is This
modalities.tagline: Stay inside a feeling and sense how long you have known it.
modalities.whatItIs: How Old Is This is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from action plans and from stepping back to watch your thoughts. Instead of observing a feeling from a distance and turning it into a next step, you let yourself be fully inside its bodily sense and gently notice whether it feels new or long familiar.
modalities.coreIdea: Many bodily feelings carry a sense of age, and simply sensing how familiar a feeling is, without acting on it, may give it room to be understood.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for about 20 minutes, let the bodily sense of a current feeling fill your attention, and stay inside it rather than watching it. Then quietly ask "how old does this feel?", receive whatever comes (a year, a place or just "very old") without searching for a memory behind it, and finish without making any plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice the same feelings returning and want a calm, self-led way to sense where they come from without analyzing them.
modalities.cautions: It works only with what you already remember: whatever comes, such as an age, a place or an image, is treated as a feeling rather than evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events. Go slowly, stop if it gets intense, and take painful memories that keep surfacing to a trauma-trained therapist rather than working them alone; it is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Ever had a feeling that seems older than the situation? New concept: How Old Is This. You stay inside a feeling's bodily sense and simply ask how old it feels, with no plan and no digging for memories. A quiet, self-led check. Untested.

modalities.name: What Your Face Holds
modalities.tagline: Feel your face from the inside; let it show your mood.
modalities.whatItIs: What Your Face Holds is a new concept that moves Focusing far from therapist-led work that searches for the hidden emotional reason behind a symptom, toward the plain, present feel of your own face. Alone, you sense from the inside what your face is doing, such as a set jaw, raised brows or a held smile, and let a felt sense of how you are come from there.
modalities.coreIdea: The face often keeps an expression we have stopped noticing, and feeling it from the inside, without explaining it, may show a mood before the mind names it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie quietly for 10 minutes with your eyes closed and slowly notice your forehead, eyes, cheeks, mouth and jaw without moving them on purpose. Ask "what expression am I wearing, and what is it like?", let a word come (braced, polite, tired), and let the face soften or stay as it is.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who smile through the day or clench without noticing, and want a quick, self-led check they can do anywhere.
modalities.cautions: Jaw or face pain that persists, or teeth grinding, is worth checking with a dentist or doctor. Feelings can surface unexpectedly; it is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Your face may be wearing an expression you stopped noticing hours ago. New concept: What Your Face Holds. Eyes closed, feel your jaw, brows and mouth from the inside, and let one word for your mood come from there. Solo and quick.

modalities.name: Fitting Image Pairs
modalities.tagline: Two friends take turns finding the image that fits a feeling.
modalities.whatItIs: Fitting Image Pairs is a new concept that moves Focusing away from body exercises and toward images and words. Two people take turns: the explorer lets the felt sense of a situation show up as a metaphor (a kind of weather, a place, an object) while the other listens and reflects it back.
modalities.coreIdea: A well-fitting metaphor can hold a vague feeling better than a list of sensations, and checking that it fits may open the situation up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Meet a trusted partner for about 40 minutes and take turns of 15 to 20 minutes each. The explorer asks "if this situation were weather or a place, what would it be?" and checks the image against their inner sense until it fits, while the listener only repeats back the images and adds no advice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body sensations hard to read but think easily in pictures, and who like exploring with a friend.
modalities.cautions: Images can lead into painful memories, so either partner can pause or stop at any time, and listeners should not interpret or push. People with severe trauma, psychosis or dissociation should explore with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: Fitting Image Pairs, a new idea: two friends take turns finding the image (a kind of weather, a place, an object) that fits a vague feeling, and the listener just reflects it back. For people who think in pictures more than sensations.

modalities.name: Pull and Hold-Back Map
modalities.tagline: For each option, feel what draws you and what holds you back.
modalities.whatItIs: Pull and Hold-Back Map is a speculative, self-run practice that pushes Focusing away from coach-led depth work and toward everyday decisions. Instead of asking the body for a single yes or no, you sense two separate felt senses for every option, the pull toward it and the hold-back from it, and lay them side by side.
modalities.coreIdea: Most options carry both attraction and reluctance, and feeling each one separately may show what a choice really involves, rather than handing you a verdict.
modalities.whatYouDo: Write each option at the top of a page with two columns, pull and hold-back. For each option, spend about two minutes sensing what in your body draws you toward it and two minutes on what holds you back, noting a word or two in each column, then read the whole map and choose one small next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get stuck going back and forth on decisions and want a structured, do-it-yourself way to include how they feel.
modalities.cautions: A felt sense is information, not a verdict, so weigh the map with facts and advice, especially for money, health or legal decisions. It is a new, untested practice, and a life crisis calls for support from people you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice: the Pull and Hold-Back Map. For each option you're weighing, spend two minutes feeling what draws you toward it and two on what holds you back, then read the whole map. Not a verdict from your gut, a fuller picture.

modalities.name: Weekly Felt Step
modalities.tagline: Each week, one small step the body proposes, then checked together.
modalities.whatItIs: Weekly Felt Step is a new concept that takes Focusing in the opposite direction from open, instruction-free meditation: more structure, a partner and more willingness to change something. Each week you meet one practice partner, let a felt sense propose one small real-life step, try it, and check next time how it felt.
modalities.coreIdea: Change may stick better when each step is chosen by the body and then felt again afterwards, in a steady weekly loop.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a partner, both taught the format by a Focusing teacher, meet for an hour a week and take 30-minute turns. Each turn starts by sensing how last week's step felt, then lets a felt sense of the current situation form, asks "what small step would feel right?" and ends with that step written down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who gain insight easily but struggle to turn it into action, and who like a clear routine with one steady partner.
modalities.cautions: Steps should be small and safe, and old patterns that surface may need a therapist rather than a peer partner. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for treatment, and either partner can pause the arrangement at any time.
modalities.tweet: From insight to action, one small step a week. Weekly Felt Step is a new idea: with one partner, you check how last week's step felt, then let your body propose the next one. A slow, structured loop from feeling to doing.

modalities.name: Room for Mixed Feelings
modalities.tagline: Let love and resentment sit side by side, unresolved.
modalities.whatItIs: Room for Mixed Feelings is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from meditations that build one warm feeling. Instead of growing goodwill, you sense the whole tangle of a situation in the body, such as love and resentment together, and let both be there without resolving them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many situations feel two ways at once, and allowing the mixed bodily sense, instead of forcing one pleasant feeling, may be more honest and less tiring.
modalities.whatYouDo: Bring to mind a person or situation you feel torn about and, for about 20 minutes, notice where each feeling sits in the body. A quiet companion can sit with you and only say back what you name, and you end by acknowledging that both feelings are present, with nothing decided.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty about having mixed feelings toward family, partners or work, and want a gentle way to let them be.
modalities.cautions: Sitting with conflicted feelings about close people can stir grief or anger, so keep sessions short and stop if it becomes overwhelming. If a relationship involves abuse or danger, safety and professional support come first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Love and resentment at the same time? New concept: Room for Mixed Feelings. Instead of trying to feel only kindness, you notice where each feeling sits in your body and let both stay. For anyone torn about someone close.

modalities.name: One Chapter, One Feeling
modalities.tagline: Feel a whole period of your life at once, then title it.
modalities.whatItIs: One Chapter, One Feeling is a new concept that pushes Focusing away from precise, structured observation of sensations and toward meaning and story. You take a whole period of your life, such as a year, a job or a move, and let a single felt sense of that chapter form while a friend listens.
modalities.coreIdea: A chapter of life can be felt all at once as a bodily whole, and finding words or images for it may clarify what that time meant.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trusted listener, spend 30 to 40 minutes on one chapter: name it, let its overall felt sense form, then let images, titles or phrases come and check each against that sense. The listener reflects back only your words, and afterwards you write a short title for the chapter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People at a turning point, such as a breakup, a career change or a big birthday, who want to make sense of a period of their life.
modalities.cautions: Choose a chapter you already remember well and feel ready for: the images that come are treated as feelings about that time, not evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to fill in forgotten parts. Stop if you feel flooded, and people with traumatic histories should do this with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: feel a whole year of your life all at once. One Chapter, One Feeling has you sense one chapter (a job, a move, a relationship) as a single bodily feeling and find its title, with a friend listening.

modalities.name: First Minutes Awake
modalities.tagline: Before the phone and the day's thinking, sense how you are.
modalities.whatItIs: First Minutes Awake is a speculative practice that moves Focusing as far as possible from bursts of intense effort, into the calmest moment of the day. In the first minutes after waking, still lying down and before any screen, you let a felt sense form of how you are and of the day ahead, while dream fragments and old moods are still near.
modalities.coreIdea: Just after waking, before the busy mind takes over, feelings that are usually drowned out may be easier to sense.
modalities.whatYouDo: When you wake, stay lying down with your eyes closed for 10 minutes, with the phone out of reach. Let a felt sense of how you are and of the coming day form, welcome any image or mood left from the night without analyzing it, and jot one word on a bedside notepad before you get up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days start at full speed with messages and news, and who want a quiet, self-led check-in before that happens.
modalities.cautions: Waking moods can be heavy, so if you regularly wake with dread or very low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist. Do not use it as a reason to stay in bed when that makes you feel worse; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Before your phone tells you how the day is going, check how you are. First Minutes Awake, a new idea: stay lying down for ten minutes after waking, let the feeling of the day ahead form, jot one word, then get up.

modalities.name: The Someday List
modalities.tagline: Feel each thing you keep saying you will do someday.
modalities.whatItIs: The Someday List is a new concept that moves Focusing far from teams and shared goals, into private, imagined futures. Alone, you write down the things you keep saying you will do someday, then let a felt sense form for each one, noticing which still feel alive and which belong to an older version of you.
modalities.coreIdea: Someday plans often carry old hopes and expectations, and sensing each one may show which of them still belong to you.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the basic Focusing steps from a book or teacher, sit alone and list five to ten somedays, such as learning the piano or moving abroad. Picture each one for a minute or two, notice its felt sense (light, heavy, guilty, warm), write one word beside it, and then let the list be without deciding anything.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry long lists of unrealized plans, and anyone at a turning point who wants to sort old hopes from current ones.
modalities.cautions: Old dreams can stir grief or regret, so go gently and talk to someone you trust if it leaves you low. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Learn the piano, move abroad, write the book: most of us carry a someday list. New idea: The Someday List. Alone, feel each item in your body and notice which still feel alive and which belong to an older you.

modalities.name: The Phrase You Keep Saying
modalities.tagline: Feel what lives under a stock phrase you say every day.
modalities.whatItIs: The Phrase You Keep Saying is a speculative practice that takes Focusing away from steady, solitary effort and toward a small everyday clue: a stock phrase you keep using, such as "I'm fine", "it's nothing" or "sorry". Having learned the steps from a Focusing teacher, you sit with a friend and let the felt sense under that phrase form.
modalities.coreIdea: Phrases we repeat without thinking may carry old feelings, and sensing what sits under one may let it be heard without any need to change how you speak.
modalities.whatYouDo: Ask a friend which phrase you say most, or notice it yourself, then meet that friend for 30 minutes. Say the phrase slowly a few times, let the felt sense under it form and say whatever comes, including any sense of where you learned it, while the friend only listens; there is no aim to stop using the phrase.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about their own habits of speech, and anyone who says "I'm fine" without being sure they are.
modalities.cautions: Any sense of where a phrase was learned comes only from what you already remember, is taken as a feeling rather than evidence of what happened, and is never a reason to search for forgotten events. Take painful memories to a therapist rather than working them through with a friend; it is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: "I'm fine." "It's nothing." "Sorry." An idea: The Phrase You Keep Saying. With a listening friend, you repeat your most-used stock phrase slowly and feel what lives underneath it. No rule to stop saying it, just curiosity. Untested.

modalities.name: Soft Spot Company
modalities.tagline: Keep your tired, tender places company, with nothing to improve.
modalities.whatItIs: Soft Spot Company is a speculative practice that moves Focusing as far as possible from building strength and tracking progress. You turn kindly toward the places where you feel weak, tired or tender and keep them company without trying to make them stronger.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting weakness and tenderness be felt, rather than overcome, may ease the strain of always having to be strong.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 20 minutes and ask where in your body or your life you feel soft, tired or fragile right now. Rest your attention there as you would sit with a tired friend, let images or memories come if they do, and set no goal and keep no record.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always the strong one, or who push through everything, and want a gentle, self-led way to let themselves be tired.
modalities.cautions: Old hurts can surface when you turn toward tender places, so go slowly, stop if it becomes too much, let only memories you already have come, take them as feelings rather than evidence of what happened, and never use the practice to search for forgotten events. See a therapist if painful feelings persist, and tiredness that does not lift can have medical causes worth checking with a doctor; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For people who are always the strong one: Soft Spot Company, a new concept. Lie down, find where you feel tired or tender, and keep that place company, with no goal of getting stronger and nothing to track.

modalities.name: The Scene That Always Lands
modalities.tagline: Feel why one scene in a story moves you every time.
modalities.whatItIs: The Scene That Always Lands is a new concept that takes Focusing away from contact with a real, living companion and into the imagined world of stories. Alone, you recall a scene from a film, book or song that moves you every time, and let the felt sense of being moved show what it touches in you.
modalities.coreIdea: When a scene moves us again and again, it is often touching something of our own, and sensing that feeling directly may let it be known.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 15 to 20 minutes and replay in your mind a scene that always gets to you, such as a reunion, a goodbye or someone finally being understood. Notice where in the body it lands, find a word or image for that feeling, and gently ask what in your own life it is near, without needing an answer.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cry at films or songs without knowing why, and anyone who finds it easier to feel through stories than through their own memories.
modalities.cautions: A moving scene can open real grief, so stop if it becomes too much and seek support if sadness lingers. Whatever the scene seems near in your own life comes from memories you already have, is taken as a feeling rather than evidence of what happened, and is never a reason to search for forgotten events; it is an untested idea and not a substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Is there a film scene that gets you every single time? Proposed practice: The Scene That Always Lands. Replay it in your mind, notice where it lands in your body, and ask gently what in your own life it is near. A new, solo idea.

modalities.name: Ask, Then Wait
modalities.tagline: Pause mid-conversation to ask how it feels, and actually wait.
modalities.whatItIs: Ask, Then Wait is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from set forms and formal sessions into ordinary conversation. Friends or family agree that, while talking over tea or a meal, any of them can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and wait for the answer.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner listening does not need a ritual; a shared habit of pausing in everyday talk can bring the felt sense into daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Agree on the habit with one or two people you talk with regularly. When someone speaks about something that matters, another asks how it feels in them, both pause for a few breaths while the speaker checks inside, and the conversation carries on, sometimes in a new direction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the idea of inner listening but will never sit down for a formal session, and households that want warmer conversations.
modalities.cautions: Not every moment suits inner questions, so anyone can decline, and the habit should never be used to pressure or analyze someone. Serious distress needs proper support; this is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Ask, Then Wait. Over tea or dinner, friends can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and actually wait for the answer. No formal session, no technique. Just slower, warmer conversations at home.

modalities.name: Region by Region Sensing
modalities.tagline: Visit six body regions in order and map how you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Region by Region Sensing is a new concept that takes Focusing away from social contact and into a quiet, structured solo routine. Lying alone, you visit regions of the body in a set order and let a small felt sense form in each one, building a private map of how you are.
modalities.coreIdea: Each part of the body can hold its own felt sense of your life, and visiting them in a set order may reveal patterns that a single check misses.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the routine from a teacher, lie down alone for 30 minutes and move through six regions (feet and legs, belly, chest, throat, face, back), asking each "what is the sense here about my life right now?". Write one word per region, and over the weeks look back at how the map changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who need solitude to recharge and like a calm, orderly practice they can do alone.
modalities.cautions: This is not a medical check, so new or persistent pain needs a doctor. Some body areas can hold painful associations, so skip any region that feels unsafe, and people with trauma or dissociation should work with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept for people who recharge alone: Region by Region Sensing. Lying down, you visit six body regions in order and ask each what it senses about your life now, writing one word per region. Over weeks, a private map appears.

modalities.name: Daily Prompt Card
modalities.tagline: Draw one prompt card each morning and focus on what it stirs.
modalities.whatItIs: Daily Prompt Card is a speculative practice that moves Focusing indoors and into a fixed daily routine built around imagined situations. A Focusing teacher gives you a small deck of prompt cards, such as "something I haven't said" or "a place I miss", and each day you draw one and let the felt sense it stirs form.
modalities.coreIdea: A random prompt can reach feelings you would not choose to visit, and a set daily routine keeps that reaching gentle and regular.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each morning, sit at the same table for 15 minutes, draw one card, picture what it brings to mind and follow a fixed sequence: sense, find a word, check it, write one line. Memories that come are noted rather than dug into, and once a month you bring the cards that stirred most to a session with the teacher.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like routines and small rituals, and who want a structured way to reach feelings they tend to avoid.
modalities.cautions: Some prompts can touch painful memories, so you can put a card back unread, and recurring distress belongs with a therapist. A card only calls up what you already remember, what comes is treated as a feeling rather than evidence of what happened, and the deck is never used to uncover forgotten events; it is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: a small deck of prompt cards like "a place I miss" or "something I haven't said". Daily Prompt Card is a new idea: draw one each morning, feel what it stirs, write one line. A structured, gentle daily ritual.

modalities.name: Between Us Sensing
modalities.tagline: Feel the sense of a relationship and find words for it.
modalities.whatItIs: Between Us Sensing is a new concept that takes Focusing away from raw sensory contact and toward the imagined space between you and another person. With a listener, you bring a relationship to mind, let the felt sense of "how it is between us" form and then find words for it.
modalities.coreIdea: Every relationship has its own felt sense, and naming it carefully may show what you want or fear in that relationship.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained listener, spend 45 minutes on one relationship: picture the person, notice the bodily sense of being with them and find a word or image that fits. If it echoes older relationships, notice that gently, and end by naming one thing you now know about what you want.
modalities.whoItsFor: People puzzling over a friendship, family tie or partnership who want to understand their own side before talking with the other person.
modalities.cautions: Exploring close relationships can stir old attachment pain, so if older relationships come to mind, stay with memories you already have, take images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and never use the practice to search for forgotten events. Go slowly and stop when you need to, people with trauma histories should work with a qualified therapist, and if a relationship is abusive or unsafe, contact support services; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Before talking something through with a person, try sensing your own side. Between Us Sensing is a proposed practice: picture them, feel how it is between you, and find words for it with a listener.

modalities.name: Finding Your Own Tempo
modalities.tagline: Sense the pace your body wants, and compare it with your calendar.
modalities.whatItIs: Finding Your Own Tempo is a new concept that moves Focusing away from music, with its shared, imposed rhythms, toward the body's own pace. Lying quietly alone, you let a felt sense form of the speed at which you actually want to live today, and compare it with the speed your schedule demands.
modalities.coreIdea: Much strain may come from living at a tempo the body does not choose, and sensing the gap can show where life needs to slow down or, sometimes, speed up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 20 minutes in a quiet room and ask "what pace does my body want today?", waiting for a felt answer such as slow and heavy or quick and light. Then picture your calendar for the day, notice the felt sense of its pace, let the difference between the two be felt, and note one place where you could follow your own tempo.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel rushed, out of step with their schedule, or always a beat behind or ahead.
modalities.cautions: Constantly feeling too slow or too fast can reflect fatigue, low mood or other health issues worth discussing with a doctor. It is an untested idea, and some demands cannot change, so be kind to yourself about what you can adjust.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Finding Your Own Tempo. Lie down, sense the pace your body wants today, then feel the pace of your calendar and notice the gap. One small change, chosen by feel, for people living at someone else's speed.

modalities.name: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings
modalities.tagline: Meet a coach eyes open, in the real room, right now.
modalities.whatItIs: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings is a new concept that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from structured imagery work and toward plain contact in the present. Coach and client sit facing each other with eyes open, and the session stays with what is actually here: the room, the light, each other's faces and the feelings that arise between them.
modalities.coreIdea: Being fully seen and present with another person, in real time and without inner images, may itself let held-back feelings soften.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session, you sit across from a trained coach, eyes open, and describe what you notice in the room, in your body and in being looked at kindly. There is no set sequence, and when memories or images pull you away, the coach gently invites you back to what you can see and feel now.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get lost in their heads or in the past and want a slow, warm practice of being present with another person.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at closely can feel exposing or stir old shame, so you can look away, pause or ask for more distance at any time. It is an untested idea offered as coaching, not therapy, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings. You sit with a coach, eyes open, and stay with what is actually here: the room, your body, being kindly seen. No imagery, no script. For people who live in their heads or in the past.

modalities.name: The Simplest Want
modalities.tagline: Find the simplest thing your body wants, and let it be.
modalities.whatItIs: The Simplest Want is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from negotiating between inner parts with competing wishes. A coach helps you find the single simplest want present in your body right now, such as to rest, to stretch, to be quiet or to be held, and to let it be fully felt without debate.
modalities.coreIdea: Under inner conflict there is often a very simple bodily want, and feeling it plainly, without parts arguing over it, may bring calm.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session with a trained coach, you talk about something you feel torn about, then pause and ask "what does my body simply want right now?" You let a plain answer come, notice what it is like to allow that want without acting on it or arguing with it, and the coach reflects it back in your words.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pulled in many directions inside and want a calm, present-focused way to find what is simplest.
modalities.cautions: This is coaching, not therapy, so if a want brings up strong distress, trauma memories or urges to harm yourself, contact a qualified mental health professional. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Torn inside? Under all the arguing, your body may want something very simple: rest, quiet, a stretch. The Simplest Want is a new concept where a coach helps you find that one want and let it be felt, without debate.

modalities.name: When the Body Is Done
modalities.tagline: Deep sessions that end when the body feels complete, not the clock.
modalities.whatItIs: When the Body Is Done is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from structured, time-limited, agenda-led therapy. Sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care have no agenda and no fixed end: old feelings are allowed to move through the body, and the session ends when the body itself feels settled.
modalities.coreIdea: Old emotional material may need to finish its own arc, and letting the body's sense of completion mark the end may avoid stopping halfway.
modalities.whatYouDo: You book a half-day block with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, and lie or sit comfortably while noticing what the body brings up, with the therapist reflecting what you notice and checking that you feel steady. When a wave of feeling has passed and the body feels quiet, you both agree the session is done, whether that took 50 minutes or two hours.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often feel cut off mid-feeling by the end of a 50-minute session and want deep work at the body's pace.
modalities.cautions: It works only with feelings and memories you already have, treats images and sensations as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it with breaks and a firm outer time limit, you can stop at any moment, and this untested idea is not for times of crisis or a replacement for well-tested treatments for PTSD or depression.
modalities.tweet: Fifty minutes is the clock's idea of a session, not your body's. When the Body Is Done is a new concept: deep work with a licensed therapist, trained in trauma care, that ends when your body feels settled. Untested.

modalities.name: Regrets, Felt Through
modalities.tagline: Meet old regrets in the body, without turning them into lessons.
modalities.whatItIs: Regrets, Felt Through is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from values work, action plans and the present moment, toward the past choices you regret. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you let a regret be felt in the body without having to repair it, learn from it or plan anything.
modalities.coreIdea: Regret is often rushed into lessons or pushed away, and simply letting it be felt, with steady company, may let it soften on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you bring one regret, from a recent choice to something from long ago, and describe the moment slowly. You notice where the regret sits in the body and what younger feelings it touches, while the therapist keeps the pace bearable and never asks for a lesson or a plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay old choices, carry guilt about the past, or have been told too often to "just move on".
modalities.cautions: It works only with memories you already have, treats feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it at a pace you control, you can stop at any point, and if regret comes with thoughts of suicide or self-harm, seek urgent help; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Replaying a choice you regret? What if you let it be felt in your body, slowly, beside a therapist who specializes in trauma, instead of turning it into a lesson or a plan? That is Regrets, Felt Through, a proposed practice for people told to just move on.

modalities.name: Home Ground Sessions
modalities.tagline: Coaching in the spot at home where you feel most at ease.
modalities.whatItIs: Home Ground Sessions is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from intense, symptom-focused uncovering in an unfamiliar office, toward the safety of familiar surroundings. The coach meets you, in person or by video, in the spot at home where you feel most at ease, and the session stays slow, calm and allowing.
modalities.coreIdea: Feelings may come forward more gently in a place the body already trusts, surrounded by your own sounds, smells and objects.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose your spot, such as a favorite armchair or a kitchen corner, and settle there for a 60-minute session with a trained coach. You notice what you can see, hear and feel around you, talk slowly about what is on your mind, and when a feeling stirs you let it be there in that familiar place, with nothing to work on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel tense in clinics or offices, live far from practitioners, or simply settle best at home.
modalities.cautions: Home sessions need privacy and clear professional boundaries, and in-person visits should follow the coach's safety rules. This untested coaching idea is not therapy, so trauma symptoms or a crisis call for a qualified mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: Some people only really settle at home. Home Ground Sessions is an untested idea: a coach meets you, in person or by video, in your favorite armchair, and the session stays slow and calm in the place your body already trusts.

modalities.name: Read Aloud by a Friend
modalities.tagline: Hear your own life story read aloud by someone you trust.
modalities.whatItIs: Read Aloud by a Friend is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from body exercises and toward words, memory and relationship. You write part of your life story, and a trusted friend who was not part of that history reads it aloud to you in a session led by a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, so you hear your own history in another voice.
modalities.coreIdea: Hearing your own story in someone else's voice may let you feel it as a listener would, with more compassion than you usually give yourself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Between sessions you write a few pages, however rough, about one period of your life that you already remember well. In a 90-minute session led by a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, a companion who was not involved in that period reads it slowly while you listen, and the therapist helps you notice what you feel as the words land. You can stop the reading at any line, and each session ends with time to settle.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it easier to feel for others than for themselves, and who have a trusted friend, outside the events, they would let read their story.
modalities.cautions: You write only what you already remember, the story is treated as your experience rather than evidence of what happened, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. The reader must be someone safe who was not part of that history and who keeps it private, a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads every session, and this untested idea is not for times of crisis.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Read Aloud by a Friend. You write a chapter of your life, and a trusted friend who wasn't part of it reads it aloud while a licensed therapist helps you notice what you feel. Your own story, heard in another voice.

modalities.name: Teenage Diary, Reread
modalities.tagline: Reread old diaries or letters with a therapist beside you.
modalities.whatItIs: Teenage Diary, Reread is a speculative practice that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from self-help inner listening and toward the actual words you wrote years ago. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you reread old diaries, school notebooks or letters you wrote, and notice how the person you were then feels to you now.
modalities.coreIdea: Old writing holds a younger self's feelings in their own words, and meeting them with company may let you understand that self more kindly.
modalities.whatYouDo: You bring a diary or a bundle of letters and, in weekly 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, read a short passage aloud or silently. You pause on what stirs you, notice how you feel toward the person who wrote it, and decide each week how much more to read.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who kept diaries or letters in their teens or twenties and feel curious, or uneasy, about who they were.
modalities.cautions: Old diaries show how you saw things then, so they are read alongside memories you already have, as feelings and points of view rather than proof of events, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten memories. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it, you can stop reading at any point, and this untested idea is not for times of crisis.
modalities.tweet: Still have your teenage diary somewhere? A new idea, Teenage Diary, Reread: a few pages a week, read beside a licensed clinician, noticing how the person who wrote them feels to you now.

modalities.name: The Missing Quality Circle
modalities.tagline: In a small group, feel a quality your old learning never allowed.
modalities.whatItIs: The Missing Quality Circle is a speculative practice that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from open, effortless sitting, toward deliberate, structured group work on long-held emotional learning. Each person names an old belief they already know well, such as "I have to manage everything alone", and, with the therapist's help, looks for any trace in the body of a quality that belief never allowed, like trust or ease, while the group holds quiet attention.
modalities.coreIdea: A quality an old belief never allowed may still be faintly present in the body, and finding it and staying with it, under the quiet attention of a small group, may help it feel like your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five people meet every two weeks for three hours with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care and group work, and each takes a 30-minute turn: name the belief in one sentence, then set it aside and, with the therapist's help, look for any small trace of the quality it never allowed, such as a moment of ease, and rest in that trace for as long as it lasts. Listeners stay silent until the turn ends, then each says one word for what they witnessed, and anyone can pause their turn at any moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already know their core beliefs well but find that insight alone has not changed how they feel.
modalities.cautions: The work uses only beliefs and memories you already know, treats feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. Members are screened by the licensed clinician trained in trauma who leads the group, anyone can stop at any time, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Insight isn't always enough. Picture a small group, led by a licensed therapist, where each person finds a trace of a quality their old beliefs never allowed, like ease, and rests in it while the others quietly witness. The Missing Quality Circle: a new idea.

modalities.name: Left Unsweetened
modalities.tagline: Feel the hard feelings you learned early to sweeten or hide.
modalities.whatItIs: Left Unsweetened is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from meditations that build warmth and goodwill, toward the hard feelings you learned long ago to sweeten. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you notice the early rule that turned anger into politeness or grief into gratitude, and let the feeling underneath be felt as it is.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people learned in childhood that some feelings were not welcome, and having such a feeling fully accepted by another person may contradict that old learning from the inside.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute one-to-one sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, when you catch yourself softening a feeling ("I'm not angry, just disappointed"), the therapist invites you to pause, sense what was being sweetened and notice the old sense of what would happen if you showed it. You let the plain feeling be there at a pace the therapist helps keep bearable, a trusted friend may sit in silently if you wish, and you never have to forgive, reframe or find a lesson.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pushed to be positive, forgiving or grateful, and who sense they learned early to tidy their feelings away.
modalities.cautions: The work uses only memories you already have, treats feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it, you can stop at any moment, and if anger comes with urges to harm anyone, or despair with thoughts of suicide, tell your therapist at once or contact emergency services; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: "I'm not angry, just disappointed." Left Unsweetened is a new concept: with a licensed therapist, you notice the feelings you learned early to sweeten, and let the plain feeling be felt as it is. No forced forgiveness, no lessons.

modalities.name: Lifelong Daydreams
modalities.tagline: Trace the life story of a daydream you have had for years.
modalities.whatItIs: Lifelong Daydreams is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from precise, moment-by-moment sensory observation and toward the private fantasies you have carried for years. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you tell the life story of one recurring daydream, such as being rescued, admired or far away, and feel the longing it has held at each age.
modalities.coreIdea: A daydream that has lasted since childhood may have kept a longing company all that time, and following how it grew and changed with you may let that longing be felt directly rather than only in fantasy.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, one to one or in a small group of three screened people, you talk loosely about one daydream as you remember it: the earliest age you recall having it, how its story changed as you grew, and what it seemed to give you at each age. The therapist helps you feel the longing inside it rather than analyze it, nothing is tracked between sessions, and you can pause or stop at any point.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have carried the same fantasy since childhood and are curious about what it has been holding for them.
modalities.cautions: Daydreams are treated as feelings and wishes, not as evidence of anything that happened, the work uses only memories you already have, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician trained in trauma care screens group members and leads every session, you can pause or stop at any time, and daydreaming that takes over many hours a day deserves a professional assessment; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if the daydream you've had since childhood had its own life story? Lifelong Daydreams is a proposed practice for tracing how it grew up with you, and the longing it has held, alongside a licensed therapist. An untested idea.

modalities.name: At Half Speed
modalities.tagline: Deep inner work done at half the pace of ordinary talk.
modalities.whatItIs: At Half Speed is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from fast, intense effort. Everything in the session happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence, so that deep and old feelings are only ever approached slowly and in stillness.
modalities.coreIdea: Radical slowness may be what makes deep material bearable: at half speed there is always time to notice, settle and choose whether to go on.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you sit or lie very still, and both of you speak in short phrases separated by long pauses. Whenever something old or painful stirs, the therapist slows things down further and checks that you feel steady before you stay with it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who talk fast, rush past their feelings or feel flooded when deep material comes too quickly.
modalities.cautions: It works only with memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. Slowness lowers but does not remove the intensity of deep work, so a licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it, you can stop at any time, and this untested idea is not for times of crisis or a replacement for well-tested trauma treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: At Half Speed. Deep inner work where everything happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence and a licensed clinician beside you. An idea for people who rush past their own feelings.

modalities.name: Guided Cabin Solitude
modalities.tagline: Days alone in a quiet place, with one guided talk a day.
modalities.whatItIs: Guided Cabin Solitude is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from teams, games and constant company into deep solitude. You spend a few days alone in a quiet place, letting inner images and old feelings come in their own time, and meet a licensed therapist trained in trauma care once a day to make sense of what arose.
modalities.coreIdea: Long stretches of solitude can let deep feelings surface that never appear in a busy week, and a daily meeting with a therapist gives a regular place to make sense of them.
modalities.whatYouDo: For three to five days you stay alone in a simple retreat cabin with your phone switched off and put away, spending the days resting, sitting, writing and noticing images, memories and moods. A licensed therapist trained in trauma care stays on site for the whole retreat, meets you for an hour each day with short check-ins every morning and evening, and can be reached at any hour on a landline in the cabin.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced inner explorers, not in crisis, who want an extended, solitary stretch of depth work with a safety net.
modalities.cautions: Solitude and intensive inner work can bring up fear, panic or unreal feelings, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma screens participants first, people with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should not take part without their own clinician's agreement, and you can end the stay at any time. Memories and images that surface are treated as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, nobody prompts you to search beyond memories you already have, and the stay is never used to uncover forgotten events; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: three days alone in a quiet cabin, phone off, letting old feelings surface in their own time, with a licensed therapist on site who checks in daily. Guided Cabin Solitude, an untested idea for experienced inner explorers.

modalities.name: After the Long Haul
modalities.tagline: Let a hard stretch you got through finally be over.
modalities.whatItIs: After the Long Haul is a speculative practice that takes Aletheia Coaching away from endurance training, where the point is to keep going at a steady pace, toward the moment of finally stopping. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you look back at a long, hard stretch from years ago that you already remember getting through, such as growing up beside a parent's long illness or a hard home life in your teens, and in deep rest let the feelings you set aside to keep going be felt at last.
modalities.coreIdea: Getting through a long, hard stretch often means putting feelings on hold, and the body may stay braced long after it ends; feeling what was held back, in deep calm and with steady support, may let the stretch end on the inside too.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over six to ten weekly 60-minute sessions, you begin each one by resting, lying or sitting under a blanket, then talk slowly about one part of that stretch and notice where the body still braces as if it were not over. When a set-aside feeling comes, the therapist helps you rest with it rather than push through, and you can pause or end any session whenever you need.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who got through a long, hard stretch years ago, often when they were young, and sense that part of them never stopped bracing.
modalities.cautions: It uses only memories you already have, treats feelings and images as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it at a pace you control, exhaustion that does not lift can have medical causes worth checking with a doctor, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis or while the hard stretch is still going on.
modalities.tweet: Some people got through years of something hard, often as kids, by just keeping going. After the Long Haul, an untested idea, offers deep rest with a trauma-trained therapist so the feelings put on hold back then can finally be felt.

modalities.name: Your Body in Old Eyes
modalities.tagline: Meet the oldest picture of your body, and leave it unchanged.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Body in Old Eyes is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as it can go from strength training, which sets out to reshape the body through effort, numbers and steady progress. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you work in words and images, never exercise, with the oldest picture of your body you carry, the one formed by how others looked at it and spoke about it when you were young, and you leave both that picture and your body exactly as they are.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training changes the body in the hope of feeling different about it; this goes the other way, on the idea that how you see your body may still follow a picture formed early by other people's looks and words, and that meeting that picture slowly, with no aim to improve it or you, may loosen its hold.
modalities.whatYouDo: Weekly 60-minute sessions have no set steps beyond a few quiet minutes of settling at the start and end: sitting comfortably and fully clothed, you put into words the picture of your body you grew up with, such as "the clumsy one" or "too big", and the remarks or looks you already remember that shaped it, and let whatever feeling comes be there. Nothing is weighed, measured or looked at in a mirror, the therapist never offers a kinder picture or asks you to replace it, and you can pause, change topic or stop whenever you need.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who still see their body the way it was described to them as a child, even when they know that picture is out of date.
modalities.cautions: It uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it at a pace you control, you can stop at any point, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis or as a substitute for specialist treatment of an eating disorder or body dysmorphia.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea for anyone who still sees their body the way it was described to them as a kid: Your Body in Old Eyes. You talk that old picture through, slowly, with a licensed trauma therapist. Nothing weighed, nothing to improve.

modalities.name: Childhood Rooms Revisited
modalities.tagline: A guided imagined walk through the rooms you grew up in.
modalities.whatItIs: Childhood Rooms Revisited is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from outward contact with real companions and toward inner imagery of the past. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you imagine walking through the rooms of a home you grew up in and notice the felt sense each room brings.
modalities.coreIdea: Places hold feelings, and slowly revisiting remembered rooms in imagination may bring old emotional learnings gently into awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions, a licensed therapist trained in trauma care invites you to picture the front door of a childhood home and move at your own pace from room to room, describing what you see and feel in the body. You choose which doors to open and can step back outside at any moment, and the therapist never suggests what you should find.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about how their early home shaped their feelings today, who think easily in pictures.
modalities.cautions: You visit only a home you already remember, the images are treated as feelings rather than a record of what happened, and the work is never used to uncover forgotten events, so the therapist, a licensed clinician trained in trauma, avoids leading questions. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should only do it within their own treatment, you can step back outside at any moment, and it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Think of the front door of the home you grew up in. Childhood Rooms Revisited, a new idea, is a slow imagined walk from room to room, led by a trauma-trained therapist, where you choose which doors to open.

modalities.name: Past the Practiced Story
modalities.tagline: Set aside the version of your past you always tell.
modalities.whatItIs: Past the Practiced Story is a speculative practice that pushes Aletheia Coaching as far as it can go from qigong, with its set forms repeated the same way each day, into work with no form at all. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you notice when you slip into the practiced version of your own history, the account you have given many times, and set its shape aside to feel what it is like to remember without it.
modalities.coreIdea: A history told many times can harden into a set form that keeps its feeling at a distance, and remembering without that form, slowly and with steady support, may let the feeling be met freshly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Weekly 60-minute sessions have no steps or sequence: you talk about a part of your past you already know well, and when the therapist hears the familiar phrasing, or you notice it yourself, you pause and stay with what is there before the words. You never have to retell anything in full, the old account is never argued with or corrected, and you can pause or stop whenever you need.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tell their past in the same words every time and suspect those words now keep it at arm's length.
modalities.cautions: It works only with memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events or to swap your account for a new one. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it at a pace you control, you can stop at any point, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Some stories about our past get told so often they stop being felt. An idea for that: Past the Practiced Story, slow sessions with a trauma-trained therapist where you pause each time the familiar version starts and notice what is there before the words.

modalities.name: The Therapist Next Door
modalities.tagline: An hour alone with old feelings, with your therapist next door.
modalities.whatItIs: The Therapist Next Door is a speculative practice that takes Aletheia Coaching far from conversation and company, into deep work done in private. You spend the session alone in a quiet room with whatever old feelings come, while a licensed therapist trained in trauma care waits in the next room, checks in at set times and comes the moment you call.
modalities.coreIdea: Some people can only let deep feelings come when no one is watching, and knowing skilled help is a door away may make that privacy safe enough to use.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 90-minute session starts and ends with ten minutes together with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, who then moves to the next room. In between you lie or sit and let feelings and memories come in the body, with a bell to call the therapist, who also knocks gently every 20 minutes to check you are steady.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who freeze or perform when watched, and who want depth work with privacy but not isolation.
modalities.cautions: Feelings and memories that come are treated as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, the work uses only memories you already have, and it is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma assesses you first, can be called in at any moment and will end the session whenever you ask, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis or for people prone to dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Can't let feelings come while someone watches? New concept: The Therapist Next Door. You spend the session alone with whatever rises, while a licensed clinician waits in the next room, checks in every 20 minutes and comes the moment you ring.

modalities.name: Kept Since Childhood
modalities.tagline: Company for a secret you have kept since you were young.
modalities.whatItIs: Kept Since Childhood is a speculative practice that takes Aletheia Coaching away from nature walks, out in open country where nothing is hidden and nothing personal is asked of you, toward the most closely held corner of a personal history. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you explore what it has been like to keep something to yourself since you were young, a family matter or something about yourself, without ever having to say what it is.
modalities.coreIdea: A secret kept since childhood can shape how you hold yourself for decades, and it may be the keeping, more than the content, that needs company: feeling what carrying it has been like, beside someone steady, may let it weigh less, whether or not you ever tell it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 60-minute session has three loose parts: you settle, then talk about the keeping itself (when you remember it beginning, what you feared would happen if it came out, where you feel it in the body), and end with a few quiet minutes. The therapist never asks what the secret is and explains at the start what they would have to act on if you chose to tell, and you alone decide whether to tell, now or ever.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have held something on their own since they were young and want company with the weight of it without having to reveal it.
modalities.cautions: It uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events or to pressure you to tell. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma leads it, you can stop at any point, if the secret involves someone being harmed now, getting safe comes first, with support services, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Kept something to yourself since you were a kid? Kept Since Childhood is a proposed practice where a licensed therapist keeps you company with the keeping itself: what carrying it has been like. You never have to say what it is.

modalities.name: Grieving What Was Missing
modalities.tagline: Mourn the care you needed early on and did not get.
modalities.whatItIs: Grieving What Was Missing is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from present sensory contact and toward something that cannot be sensed at all: what was absent. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, and a small screened group if you wish, you let yourself grieve the care, attention or safety you needed early on and did not get, without picturing it filled in.
modalities.coreIdea: Unmet early needs are often understood for years but never mourned, and grieving the absence, with others present, may let a long-held ache finally be felt.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions led by a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you name a need you already know went unmet, such as being comforted or praised, notice where its absence is felt in the body, and let the grief of it be there. In the group version, three people take turns while the others listen without comment, and anyone can pause or stop whenever they need.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already know a particular kind of care was missing early on, and have understood it for years without ever letting themselves mourn it.
modalities.cautions: The work uses only what you already know about your past, treats feelings and longings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. A licensed clinician experienced in trauma screens members and leads every session, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis or in early, acute grief.
modalities.tweet: Knowing what you missed as a child is not the same as mourning it. New concept: Grieving What Was Missing, where a licensed therapist and a small, screened group help you grieve the care you needed early on and did not get.

modalities.name: Where Feeling Went Quiet
modalities.tagline: Meet numbness as an old shield, without trying to break it.
modalities.whatItIs: Where Feeling Went Quiet is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from music, which is made to stir and share feeling, toward the places in you where feeling has gone still. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you get to know a long-standing numbness, such as feeling nothing at family gatherings, as an old shield that may have come at a time you already remember when there was too much to feel, without trying to bring feeling back.
modalities.coreIdea: Numbness is often treated as a wall to break through, yet it may have begun long ago as a shield against too much, and meeting the shield itself, with the time it comes from acknowledged, may let it ease when it is ready.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 60-minute one-to-one sessions, you sense what the numbness is like in the body, its edges and its weight, then, if one comes to mind from what you already remember, name the time in your early life it seems to come from, such as years of shouting at home, and acknowledge it as the reason the shield was needed, without going into the events themselves. The therapist never uses music, memories or exercises to provoke feeling and stays with the shield rather than what lies behind it, and you go only as far as feels bearable and can stop at any point.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel flat or far away where others seem moved, and who are tired of being told to open up.
modalities.cautions: It uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events. Lasting numbness can be part of depression, PTSD or dissociation, or a side effect of medication, so check with a doctor first; a licensed clinician experienced in trauma screens you before you start and leads every session, people prone to dissociation take part only within their own ongoing treatment, and this untested idea is not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Feel flat where everyone else seems moved? A proposed practice, Where Feeling Went Quiet, sees numbness as an old shield: with a licensed therapist, you get to know the shield and where it came from, rather than breaking through it. Untested.

modalities.name: Idle Eyes at the Window
modalities.tagline: Sit at a window, eyes open, and let looking happen.
modalities.whatItIs: Idle Eyes at the Window is a new concept that pushes Do Nothing meditation further from imagery-based therapy, toward the plain outside world. You sit at a window with your eyes open and let looking happen by itself, with no instruction from anyone, no inner pictures to build and no history to explore.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the eyes wander over the real world, without steering them or building inner images, may be one of the simplest ways to rest the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a window, sit down for 10 to 20 minutes and let your gaze go wherever it goes: clouds, a wall, passing cars, a fly. If you notice yourself trying to look properly or to meditate well, let that go too, and get up whenever you like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation strange or heavy and want a no-instruction rest they can start on their own today.
modalities.cautions: Open sitting can still let worries or difficult feelings surface; if that keeps happening, try a more guided practice or talk to someone you trust. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for anxiety or depression.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Idle Eyes at the Window. Sit at a window, eyes open, and let your gaze wander over clouds, walls and passing cars. No instructions, no visualizing, nothing to get right. A rest you can start today if eyes-closed meditation feels strange.

modalities.name: Unanswered Inner Chatter
modalities.tagline: Your running inner commentary keeps talking; you stop answering it.
modalities.whatItIs: Unanswered Inner Chatter is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapies that hold conversations with inner parts. When your ordinary running commentary worries, judges or argues, you neither answer it, nor argue back, nor try to quiet it; you let it talk like a radio in another room.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner chatter may lose some of its pull when nobody inside answers it, so not replying becomes a way to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie down for 15 minutes with your eyes open or closed and let sounds, sensations and the running commentary in your head all happen. Each time you catch yourself replying to a thought, reassuring it or arguing with it, drop the reply and let the commentary carry on unanswered.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with busy, chattering minds who are tired of arguing with their own thoughts.
modalities.cautions: If you hear voices that seem to come from outside you, or that frighten or command you, stop and speak with a doctor or mental health professional. It is an untested idea, and people with psychosis, severe trauma or dissociation should not use it in place of professional care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for chattering minds: Unanswered Inner Chatter. When your ordinary running thoughts worry or argue, you don't answer, argue back or shush them. You let them talk like a radio in the next room. For anyone tired of arguing with themselves.

modalities.name: Hammock, Nothing Else
modalities.tagline: Lie in a hammock, let it sway, and add nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Hammock, Nothing Else is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation even further from structured, scheduled therapy. You lie in a hammock, indoors or in a garden, let it sway or settle as it will, and add nothing: no timer, no technique, no book, no music.
modalities.coreIdea: A hammock holds and gently rocks the body without any effort, which may make letting go of control feel natural rather than like a task.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie in a securely hung hammock and let your body be rocked or still, with whatever thoughts, sounds and drowsiness come and go. Do not set a timer or keep a record; climb out when you feel like it, slowly, with both feet on the ground first.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sitting meditation stiff or effortful, and anyone who rests best when held and rocked.
modalities.cautions: Hang the hammock securely at a low height and get in and out carefully, since falls are the main risk, and skip it if you have dizziness or balance problems. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for stress or sleep problems.
modalities.tweet: Not everyone meditates well sitting up. Hammock, Nothing Else is a new concept: lie in a hammock, let it sway or settle, and add nothing: no timer, no technique, no book, no music. Climb out when you feel like it.

modalities.name: Nothing, Side by Side
modalities.tagline: Two people in one room, both doing nothing, no talking.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing, Side by Side is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapy built on conversation, values and plans. Two people who are at ease with each other sit in the same room and both do nothing, without talking, looking after each other or doing anything together.
modalities.coreIdea: Quiet company that asks nothing may make doing nothing feel less lonely or strange, without turning it into a shared activity.
modalities.whatYouDo: Agree with a partner, friend or housemate on 20 minutes, sit in the same room in any comfortable position, and each let whatever happens happen. There is no rule about eye contact, no sharing afterwards and no need to stay if one of you wants to stop.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find solo meditation lonely, and couples or friends who are always busy together and rarely just are together.
modalities.cautions: Choose someone you feel safe and relaxed with, and stop if the silence starts to feel tense. It is an untested idea, not a treatment, and difficult feelings that surface deserve support from someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Always busy together, never just together? An idea: Nothing, Side by Side. You and a friend or partner sit in the same room for 20 minutes, both doing nothing, no talking, no sharing afterwards. Untested, and oddly cozy.

modalities.name: The Sun Patch
modalities.tagline: Rest in a patch of sunlight, like a cat.
modalities.whatItIs: The Sun Patch is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation far from intense, therapist-led work on hidden emotional meaning, toward simple warmth and light. Whenever sunlight falls into a room, you sit or lie in the patch it makes and do nothing until it moves on.
modalities.coreIdea: Warmth and light are among the simplest comforts, and resting in them with nothing to work on may let the body settle on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a sunny day, find where light falls through a window, sit or lie in it with your eyes open or closed and let whatever happens happen. Stay as long as it feels pleasant, or until the patch has moved off you, and then get on with your day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend most of the day indoors, and anyone who wants a no-skill, no-equipment way to rest.
modalities.cautions: Strong sun through a window can overheat you, so keep sessions short in hot weather, drink water and never look straight at the sun. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care when low mood or anxiety persists.
modalities.tweet: Ever envied a cat in a sunbeam? The Sun Patch is a new idea: when sunlight falls into a room, sit or lie in it and do nothing until it moves on. No skill, no app, no equipment. Just warmth.

modalities.name: Until the Tea Cools
modalities.tagline: Do nothing until your hot drink is cool enough to sip.
modalities.whatItIs: Until the Tea Cools is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from body exercises and lets an everyday hot drink set the length. You make a cup of tea or another hot drink, sit down with it and do nothing at all until it is cool enough to drink.
modalities.coreIdea: A cooling drink gives a natural, unforced end point, so there is no timer and no technique, only a few minutes of letting the mind do what it does.
modalities.whatYouDo: Make your drink, put it down within reach and sit. You do not watch the cup, breathe in a special way or think about anything in particular: thoughts and daydreams come and go, and when the drink feels cool enough, you drink it and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who make hot drinks and then forget them while working, and anyone who wants a tiny daily rest with a built-in end.
modalities.cautions: Keep hot drinks out of reach of children and pets, and set the cup down somewhere stable while you sit. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for stress or anxiety.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Until the Tea Cools. Make a hot drink, put it down and do nothing at all until it's cool enough to sip. No timer, no technique, no staring at the cup. A tiny daily rest with a built-in end point.

modalities.name: Phoneless Café Table
modalities.tagline: Sit at a busy café with a drink and nothing else.
modalities.whatItIs: Phoneless Café Table is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from quiet, inward listening to the body and out among people. You sit at a café table with a drink, with no phone, book, laptop or company, and let the life of the place go on around you while you do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing nothing in public, silently alongside strangers, may show that rest does not need a quiet room or closed eyes.
