modalities.whatYouDo: Order something, leave the phone in your bag and sit for 20 minutes with your eyes open. Let conversations, clatter, people passing and your own thoughts come and go, and if you notice an urge to look busy or to watch people on purpose, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they can only rest at home, and anyone who reaches for a phone the moment they sit down in public.
modalities.cautions: Keep an eye on your belongings, and choose a calm café if crowds make you anxious. It is an untested idea, and if being alone in public brings strong anxiety or low mood, talking to a professional may help.
modalities.tweet: An idea: Phoneless Café Table. A drink, no phone, book or laptop, and 20 minutes letting the clatter and chatter of a café go on around you while you do nothing. New, untested and surprisingly hard.

modalities.name: Just Standing There
modalities.tagline: Stand still somewhere ordinary and do nothing for five minutes.
modalities.whatItIs: Just Standing There is a speculative practice that takes Do Nothing meditation away from long coach-guided sessions and into the plainest posture of all. Anywhere at home, you stand still for a few minutes, eyes open, and let whatever happens happen, with no special stance and no instructions from anyone.
modalities.coreIdea: Standing still without a reason is rare and slightly odd, and doing it on purpose may make doing nothing feel ordinary rather than special.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a spot, such as the middle of the kitchen or beside a window, and stand for about five minutes with your arms however they fall. Let thoughts, sounds and the small sways of the body come and go, and if you notice yourself trying to stand properly, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot sit still for meditation, or who sit all day and want a different kind of break.
modalities.cautions: Stand near something you can hold if you get dizzy, sit down if you feel faint, and skip it if standing is painful. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: When did you last stand still for no reason? An idea: Just Standing There. Five minutes standing in your kitchen, eyes open, arms however they fall, letting whatever happens happen. No special stance, nothing to get right.

modalities.name: Welcome the Boredom
modalities.tagline: Let dull, ordinary time stay dull, and stay with it.
modalities.whatItIs: Welcome the Boredom is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from practices that build up warm, pleasant feelings. Instead of cultivating goodwill or bliss, you welcome the flat, dull, boring moments that most meditation tries to get past.
modalities.coreIdea: Boredom is usually escaped within seconds, and letting it be, without making it pleasant, may make ordinary life easier to sit with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit somewhere unremarkable for 15 minutes with no phone, music or book, and let the time feel as dull as it does. When you notice an urge to make it nicer (a pleasant thought, a plan, a fidget), let the urge be and let the moment stay as flat as it is.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who reach for their phone at every quiet moment and want to get comfortable with ordinary, unexciting time.
modalities.cautions: Feeling flat for a few minutes is normal, but a lasting loss of interest or pleasure can be a sign of depression that deserves a talk with a doctor. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Welcome the Boredom is a new idea: fifteen minutes somewhere unremarkable, no phone or music, letting the time feel as dull as it is. No bliss to chase, just getting comfortable with ordinary time. 📵

modalities.name: Fog Allowed Sitting
modalities.tagline: When the mind is hazy, let it stay hazy.
modalities.whatItIs: Fog Allowed Sitting is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from insight practices that observe experience precisely. You make no attempt to see clearly: when the mind is foggy, vague or half-dreaming, you let it stay that way.
modalities.coreIdea: Demanding clarity of a tired mind can become its own strain, so allowing the fog may let rest happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 15 to 20 minutes, close your eyes or let them unfocus, and let thoughts be blurry and half-formed. You do not label, note or examine anything, and if you notice an effort to see more clearly, you drop it and let the haze be.
modalities.whoItsFor: Tired people, and meditators who feel they must always be alert and precise, who want a gentler, hazier rest.
modalities.cautions: Fogginess that lasts, or new trouble thinking clearly, can have medical causes and should be checked by a doctor. This untested idea is not for moments that need alertness, and people with dissociation should talk to a clinician before trying it.
modalities.tweet: Some days the mind is just foggy. Fog Allowed Sitting is a proposed practice that says fine, stay foggy: no noting, no examining, no effort to see clearly, just letting a hazy mind rest. A new concept for tired brains.

modalities.name: Parked Car Pause
modalities.tagline: Engine off, before you go inside: a few minutes of nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Parked Car Pause is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from intense, timed effort, into the quiet gap between parts of the day. When you arrive home or at work by car, you stay put for a few minutes with the engine off and do nothing before going in.
modalities.coreIdea: The minutes between one role and the next are usually skipped, and spending them doing nothing may let the mind arrive more fully.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you are safely parked with the engine off, put the phone in the glove box, sit back and let thoughts about where you have been and where you are going come and go for three to ten minutes. Then get out and go in, with nothing to report or record.
modalities.whoItsFor: Commuters and parents who rush straight from work into the next demand and want a small buffer.
modalities.cautions: Only do this when properly parked in a safe, well-lit place with the engine off, never on a road shoulder and never in a closed garage with the engine running. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for stress.
modalities.tweet: New idea: the Parked Car Pause. Engine off, phone in the glove box, and three to ten minutes of doing nothing before you walk in the door. A small buffer between work and whatever waits at home.

modalities.name: The Unreachable Half Hour
modalities.tagline: Thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unreachable Half Hour is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from teams, roles and constant coordination with others. For thirty minutes you make yourself completely unreachable, with phone off and door closed, and do nothing at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Knowing that nobody can call on you, even briefly, may let the part of the mind that is always on standby switch off.
modalities.whatYouDo: Tell anyone who depends on you that you will be unavailable for half an hour, switch your phone off (not just to silent) and close the door. Sit or lie however you like and let whatever happens happen, until the half hour is over.
modalities.whoItsFor: Parents, carers, managers and anyone who is always on call and rarely has time that belongs to nobody else.
modalities.cautions: Only do this when someone else is covering anyone who needs supervision, such as young children or a person you care for. Solitude can let low mood surface, so if it regularly leaves you feeling worse, talk to someone; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For parents, carers and anyone on call, an idea: The Unreachable Half Hour. Phone off (not on silent), door closed, someone else covering, and thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you. Untested, but easy to try.

modalities.name: Nowhere to Get To
modalities.tagline: Turn queues, platforms and waiting rooms into rest.
modalities.whatItIs: Nowhere to Get To is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from steady effort toward a distant goal. It uses the moments when you are stuck waiting, in queues, on platforms or in waiting rooms, as a chance to stop trying to get anywhere and let whatever happens happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Waiting is usually spent straining toward what comes next, and dropping that strain may turn dead time into rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Learn the idea from a short guide or book, then each time you have to wait, leave your phone in your pocket and stop willing the wait to end. Let your eyes, thoughts and impatience do whatever they do, and when the bus, the queue or the appointment arrives, simply carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Impatient people, commuters and anyone who loses a lot of time to waiting and finds it irritating.
modalities.cautions: Stay aware of your surroundings, your belongings and any traffic, and never do this while driving or cycling. It is an untested idea, and impatience that comes with intense anger or anxiety may deserve professional support.
modalities.tweet: Stuck in a queue again? New idea: Nowhere to Get To. Each time you have to wait, phone stays in your pocket and you stop willing the wait to end. Let thoughts and impatience do what they do. Dead time, turned into rest.

modalities.name: The Unplanned Saturday
modalities.tagline: One whole day off with nothing planned, left to unfold.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unplanned Saturday is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from programs, progress and effort, and stretches it across a whole day. Once in a while you keep a day off completely free, with no plans, chores, goals or bookings, and let the day happen without steering it.
modalities.coreIdea: A day with no plan is rarely allowed in busy lives, and letting one unfold on its own may show what the mind does when nothing is asked of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, pick a day, clear the calendar, tell people you are unavailable and wake without an alarm. Through the day you rest, drift or do whatever small thing comes, and whenever you notice yourself making a plan or a to-do list, you let that intention go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose weekends fill up as fast as their weekdays, and anyone who has forgotten what an empty day feels like.
modalities.cautions: An empty day can let low mood or loneliness surface, so keep an easy way to reach someone if it feels heavy. It is an untested idea, and essential care for children, pets or your health still comes first.
modalities.tweet: New idea: The Unplanned Saturday. One day off with no plans, chores or bookings, no alarm and no to-do list, just letting the day unfold. An untested experiment for people whose weekends fill up as fast as their weekdays.

modalities.name: Daytime Dark Room
modalities.tagline: Sit in a darkened room by day, eyes open, and do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Daytime Dark Room is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from warm contact with a living companion, toward solitude with nothing to see. In the daytime, you darken a room as fully as you can and sit in it with your eyes open, letting whatever the mind and the dark bring come and go.
modalities.coreIdea: With nothing to look at, there is little to steer toward, and inner pictures, thoughts and stillness can simply come and go.
modalities.whatYouDo: Draw the blinds or curtains, switch off screens and lights, and sit or lie down for 15 minutes with your eyes open in the dark. Let shapes, inner images, sounds and thoughts appear and fade, and when you are ready, let the light back in slowly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation sleepy or strange, and anyone curious about what the mind does with nothing to see.
modalities.cautions: Darkness can stir fear or distressing memories for some people, so keep a light switch within reach and stop if it feels frightening. Move carefully in the dark to avoid trips; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What does your mind do with nothing to look at? New concept: Daytime Dark Room. Blinds down, lights off, eyes open, fifteen minutes in the dark in the middle of the day, letting whatever comes come and go.

modalities.name: Slumped and Unposed
modalities.tagline: No posture, no breathing technique: rest exactly as you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Slumped and Unposed is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from careful postures and regulated breathing. You sit or sprawl in whatever position you happen to be in, slumped on the sofa if that is where you are, and leave the breath and body alone entirely.
modalities.coreIdea: Arranging the body and breath can quietly turn rest into a performance, so leaving them unarranged may remove one more layer of control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Wherever you are sitting or lying, stop for 10 to 20 minutes without straightening up, closing your eyes or adjusting your breath. Let attention drift through thoughts and daydreams, and when you catch yourself fixing your posture or breathing deeply on purpose, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they cannot meditate because they cannot sit still or upright, and anyone put off by strict postures.
modalities.cautions: Shift position if something starts to ache or go numb, since leaving the body alone does not mean staying in pain. It is an untested idea, and anyone with breathing problems or chronic pain should follow their own clinician's advice.
modalities.tweet: Good news for sofa sprawlers. Slumped and Unposed is a new idea: stay exactly as you are, leave your breath and posture alone, and let your mind drift. No performance, no technique.

modalities.name: Talk-Free Evening
modalities.tagline: An evening of not speaking after a socially full week.
modalities.whatItIs: Talk-Free Evening is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from talk and social contact. After days full of people, you spend an evening alone without speaking, messaging or listening to talk, and simply let the quiet be.
modalities.coreIdea: Speech keeps the social mind running, and a stretch of not talking at all may let it wind down more fully than ordinary rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you have learned the idea from a short guide, pick an evening, tell the people you live with, and put away your phone and anything with voices in it. Move slowly through ordinary things like making tea or lying on the bed, and in between, sit and do nothing until bedtime.
modalities.whoItsFor: Introverts, people in people-heavy jobs and anyone who feels talked out by the end of the week.
modalities.cautions: Make sure someone can still reach you in an emergency, and do not use silence to avoid people you need to talk to. If you avoid company because of fear or low mood, or the quiet makes you feel worse, talk to a doctor or therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: After a week full of people, try the Talk-Free Evening, a new concept: no speaking, no messaging, no podcasts, just moving slowly through tea and quiet and doing nothing until bed. An untested idea for introverts.

modalities.name: Snug Corner Pause
modalities.tagline: Tuck yourself into a small, sheltered corner and do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Snug Corner Pause is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from open landscapes and walking, into a small, enclosed indoor space. You set up a snug corner, such as a window seat, a deep armchair with a blanket or a gap between shelves, and go there only to do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: A small, sheltered space can feel protective, and keeping one spot just for doing nothing may make it easier to stop.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, choose and arrange your nook with a cushion and a blanket, and visit it for 15 minutes when you need a break. Inside, you let thoughts, daydreams and sounds come and go without steering them, and you keep phones, books and work out of the nook.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find open spaces or bare rooms hard to relax in, and anyone who loved dens and cozy corners as a child.
modalities.cautions: Enclosed spaces can feel uncomfortable for people with claustrophobia, so keep the nook open on one side and leave whenever you like. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for anxiety.
modalities.tweet: Proposed practice for anyone who loved building dens as a kid: Snug Corner Pause. Set up a snug corner with a cushion and blanket, keep phones and work out, and go there only to do nothing for 15 minutes. A new idea.

modalities.name: After the Last Page
modalities.tagline: When a story ends, sit a while before starting the next.
modalities.whatItIs: After the Last Page is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from the senses and into the imagination a story leaves behind. When you finish a book, film or episode, you do not reach for the next one; you sit for a while doing nothing and let the story's images and feelings linger or fade on their own.
modalities.coreIdea: Stories leave an afterglow that is usually cut short by the next thing, and staying with it without steering may be a rest in itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, close the book or switch off the screen at the end, stay seated and keep the room quiet for 10 minutes. Scenes, characters and feelings may replay, drift or vanish, and you neither analyze them nor push them away; then you get up and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Readers and viewers who binge one story after another and rarely let any of them land.
modalities.cautions: Sad or frightening stories can leave you low or unsettled, so if the afterglow is distressing, turn on a light, move around or talk to someone. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: When a story ends, don't start the next one yet. After the Last Page is a new concept: stay seated for ten quiet minutes and let the scenes and feelings linger or fade on their own. An idea for bingers.

modalities.name: Unmasked Everyday Noise
modalities.tagline: Stop masking everyday noise: hear it and do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Unmasked Everyday Noise is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from music and toward the plain, unmasked sound of daily life. Instead of covering traffic, neighbors or office hum with music or podcasts, you take the headphones off, sit, and let ordinary noise be heard while you do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: Many of us mask the world's sounds all day, and letting them in, unedited and unchosen, may make daily noise feel less like something to escape.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a day, in a place with ordinary background noise, take off your headphones, put the phone away and sit for 10 to 15 minutes. Let sounds you like and sounds you do not like come and go, along with any irritation they bring, without reaching for anything to cover them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who wear headphones most of the day and find everyday noise hard to bear.
modalities.cautions: Do not do this in places with harmfully loud noise, and protect your hearing where volume is high. If sounds feel unbearable or trigger distress, it may be sound sensitivity worth discussing with a doctor; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: An idea: Unmasked Everyday Noise. Headphones off for ten minutes a day, sitting with ordinary noise (traffic, neighbors, office hum) while you do nothing. A new concept for people who block the world out all day.
